```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5
)
```

Each step of the workflow is a separate function that returns an object.
`print()` shows the results as a table and `autoplot()` plots them.

```{r}
library(envirolipids)
```

# Describe the data

Data need one column per brGDGT compound (`fIa`, `fIb`, `fIc`, `fIIa`, `fIIa_`,
`fIIb`, `fIIb_`, `fIIc`, `fIIc_`, `fIIIa`, `fIIIa_`, `fIIIb`, `fIIIb_`,
`fIIIc`, `fIIIc_`), as fractions (summing to 1) or percentages (summing to 100),
plus optionally a sample `ID` column. The example data come from a sediment
core with ages.

```{r}
data(example_data)
head(example_data)
```

A quick summary of the composition, by compound and by methylation group:

```{r}
brgdgt_cols <- c("fIa", "fIb", "fIc", "fIIa", "fIIa_", "fIIb", "fIIb_",
                 "fIIc", "fIIc_", "fIIIa", "fIIIa_", "fIIIb", "fIIIb_",
                 "fIIIc", "fIIIc_")
round(sapply(example_data[, brgdgt_cols], range), 3)

methylation <- brgdgt_methylation(example_data)
summary(methylation[, c("tetra", "penta", "hexa")])
```

# Check applicability

Before predicting NPP, check whether the samples fall within the brGDGT
composition space of the training data.

```{r}
check <- npp_brgdgt_applicable(example_data, threshold = 0.95, n_neighbors = 5)
check
```

The per-sample table is available with `as.data.frame(check)`, and the
nearest training samples for each sample with `check$neighbours`.

```{r, fig.cap = "Mahalanobis distances to the training data"}
autoplot(check, type = "mahalanobis")
```

```{r, fig.cap = "PCA of samples vs training data"}
autoplot(check, type = "pca")
```

```{r, fig.cap = "Methylation groups (training data sized by NPP)"}
autoplot(check, type = "ternary")
```

```{r, fig.cap = "Training sites with most similar brGDGT composition", eval = requireNamespace("maps", quietly = TRUE)}
autoplot(check, type = "map")
```

# Predict NPP from brGDGTs

```{r}
npp <- npp_brgdgt(example_data, sample_type = "Lacustrine Sediment")
head(npp)
```

```{r, fig.cap = "brGDGT-based NPP through time"}
autoplot(npp, x = example_data$Age, xlab = "Age (years BP)")
```

`temp_brgdgt()` predicts mean annual temperature with the same interface,
once the temperature model is available.

# Potential NPP from climate

When mean annual temperature and total annual precipitation are available
(here simulated),
potential NPP can be estimated with the Miami model or the Thornthwaite
Memorial model.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
mat <- seq(10, 15, length.out = 50) + rnorm(50, 0, 1)
map <- seq(400, 700, length.out = 50) + rnorm(50, 0, 100)

miami <- npp_miami(mat, map, id = example_data$ID)
head(miami)

thornthwaite <- npp_thornthwaite(mat, map, id = example_data$ID)
head(thornthwaite)
```

```{r, fig.cap = "Potential NPP from the Miami model"}
autoplot(miami, x = example_data$Age, xlab = "Age (years BP)")
```

# NPP deficit (HANPP)

The difference between climate-based and brGDGT-based NPP shows where NPP
departs from climatic expectations, e.g. through human appropriation of NPP.

```{r}
deficit <- hanpp(npp_empirical = npp, npp_model = miami)
head(deficit)
```

```{r, fig.cap = "Comparison of NPP estimates"}
autoplot(deficit, x = example_data$Age, xlab = "Age (years BP)")
```
